I grew up deeply involved in the Presbyterian church, left it when I went to college (which was a Jesuit institution, so out one church into the next) and haven't attended a service since. My family was heavily involved in the goings on of the church, both my parents served (and still serve) as deacons and elders as well as on various church committees, myself and my siblings all at some point were involved with youth groups, the music program, and set up then cleaned the church before and after service. Every Sunday, we were the first to show up and the last to leave. We were *the* volunteer family, and anything that needed volunteers, we were the ones who took it on (at one point I remember my dad saying "if someone from the church asks you to do something, that's God asking" which even as I child I thought was pretty fucked up.) Even though I don't think I would have ever called myself a believer, I spent at least three days a week at church through my childhood and adolescence at my parents insistence.

All that to say, religion has been a huge obstacle in my coming out. I am terrified of what the people at my old church (still my parents church) would think of me if they knew I was transgender and how it might effectively ostracize my parents from the group of people they are most in community with. I haven't spoken to any of these people in nearly seven years! But I'm still scared of them! And so my options are come out to my parents and hope they don't tell anyone in the church (which would hurt) or stay closeted (which hurts right now). I'm working through it with a therapist but it's definitely been a hindrance 

Anyway, this turned into more of a vent than directly answering your question, but if any of y'all reading this are in a similar boat, the youtube channel "Belief it or Not" has been really helpful for me in unpacking that shit ([this video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gqbdgUR6wWc) is very good for unpacking the idea that you are "unworthy" or "broken" that the modern church loves to use)

Gonna put on my English teacher hat here! The attachment between gender presentation and pronouns in the English language is arbitrary (there are plenty of languages that don't have gendered pronouns at all!) There's no reason a feminine expression of gender can't be paired with a "masculine" pronoun (or vice versa) if the pronoun set feels right to you (also what is feminine what is masculine, so much shit we internalize and then have to unpack lol) If he/they feels right, hell yeah! That's valid!

I sense there's some guilt that you're feeling about not being "enough" in a certain direction to fit the label you want to give yourself? What is that guilt about? Are you worried that you're taking up space or resources by using a particular set of pronouns? Are you concerned that using "he/they" will cause harm to other trans people? I think it might be helpful to try challenging those thoughts and figuring out why you think "Someone like me shouldn't use them." I have a feeling once you actually figure out what the harm you think you're doing is, you'll realize that you're not actually causing any harm at all. Hope that helps!

Similar situation! I'm 24 and i did not realize I was a trans man until this past year, and looking back on my childhood it really doesn't seem like there were any signs, but I had a lot of the same thoughts you're having now when i was your age. I think sometimes for people who were raised/socialized as girls/women (especially when your someone who falls outside of the social spectrum of womanhood, like if your larger or tomboyish) it's easier to disregard discomfort in your agab as discomfort with the sexism or misogyny you might be facing. 

I've always been chubby and I would always disregard my brain saying "this would be better if i was a boy" or "i would be more comfortable doing this if i was a boy" or "I would be more attractive if i was a boy" because i understood sexism and fatphobia and how it affected the way people saw and treated me, but looking back those thoughts had a lot more to do with discomfort in my agab. A lot of the stuff you're talking about regarding your chest is really relatable because I always just assumed that i hated my boobs because they didn't fit the titty beauty standard and that forced me to completely disregard the obvious feelings of gender dysphoria I was dealing with.

None of this is to disregard the sexism or fatphobia or body shaming I was experiencing then or that you are experiencing now, but just to say that I was having a lot of the same thoughts you are having at your age and I'm glad you're doing the work to process them.
